title: From a problem to a model
subtitle: Chapter 1
outcomes: Translate a decision into variables, an objective and constraints.
Use break-even and airline-pricing models to compare alternatives.

topics.title: The management science approach
topics.body:
Management science uses mathematical models and evidence to support decisions. The course also calls it operations research, quantitative methods and business analytics. Pricing, production, logistics, scheduling and ranking all fit this approach.
Start by observing a problem. Define the decision, its boundaries and the organization’s objective. Construct a model; solve it; then implement and check the decision in its actual setting. A mathematically optimal answer is useful only if the model represents the real problem.
A decision variable is something you choose. A parameter is an input you treat as given. The objective measures the result you want to maximize or minimize; constraints define the permitted choices.

sections.title: The steel-product example
sections.body:
The slide example makes a steel product that sells for $20, costs $5 to produce and needs 4 lb of steel per unit. The firm has 100 lb of steel. Its displayed formulation uses all available steel:
$$\max Z=20x-5x,\qquad4x=100.$$
Solving the displayed equation gives x = 25 units and profit $375, as shown on page 12.
Modeling note: if steel is merely available rather than required to be exhausted, write 4x ≤ 100 with x ≥ 0. Because the contribution is positive and no demand limit is stated, this alternative availability formulation has the same optimum. That inequality is an explanatory reformulation, not the equality printed in the slide.

check.question: Which is a decision variable in the steel example?
check.explanation: The model chooses production. Steel availability and selling price are parameters.

topics.title: Break-even: cost, revenue and profit
topics.body:
Fixed cost remains constant over the modeled production range. Unit variable cost is the production cost per unit. The lecture uses c_f for fixed cost, c_v for unit variable cost, p for price and v for units produced or sold. Writing F = c_f and c = c_v, its cost and profit relationships are:
$$TC=F+cv,\qquad R=pv,\qquad Z=(p-c)v-F.$$
At break-even, revenue equals total cost and profit is zero. For p > c:
$$v_{BE}=\frac{F}{p-c}.$$
Additional boundary cases: if p = c and F > 0, no finite sales volume covers fixed cost. If p < c, additional sales reduce profit. This simple model assumes that the chosen volume can be sold at the stated price.

sections.title: Western Clothing Company
sections.body:
The slide data are F = $10,000, c = $8 per pair and p = $23 per pair. The lecture reports break-even volume 10,000/(23 − 8) ≈ 666.7 pairs. A whole-unit calculation gives at least 667 sales for nonnegative profit; profit at 667 is $5.
The revenue line starts at zero, and total cost starts at fixed cost. The figures show how changing price, unit cost or fixed cost changes their crossing. The lecture cautions that a higher price can make sales harder and can require higher unit cost to improve quality. The interactive controls extend these same equations over user-selected values; they do not estimate demand.

topics.title: Airline demand and a single fare
topics.body:
The airline has 130 seats per departure and a full economy fare of $60. The observed (fare, tickets sold) pairs in the slide are (40,55), (50,40), (30,102) and (38,60). The lecture supplies a fitted demand curve; it does not require that the curve pass through every observation.
The two displayed branches meet at fare $40 and demand 50. Extending the curve with nonnegative demand and imposing the stated seat limit gives:
$$q(p)=\begin{cases}250-5p&0\le p\le40\\90-p&40\le p\le90\\0&p\ge90.\end{cases}$$
$$s(p)=\min\{130,q(p)\},\qquad R(p)=p\,s(p).$$
The zero-demand truncation and capacity-limited sales formula make the physical bounds explicit. Calculations below use the lecture's supplied curve rather than fitting a new one to the observations.

sections.title: Derive the lecture's first three pricing results
sections.body:
The comparison table reports fare $60, 30 tickets and revenue $1,800 for strategy 1. To fill the plane in strategy 2, solve 250 − 5p = 130: fare $24 gives revenue $3,120.
For strategy 3, derive the revenue maximum from the supplied curve. In the uncapped low-price region, R = 250p − 5p², with derivative 250 − 10p. At p = $25, sales are 125 and revenue is $3,125. The higher-price branch has its own stationary point at p = $45, with 45 sales and revenue $2,025. Checking the capacity breakpoint and branch boundaries confirms the best common fare of $25, matching the lecture's table.
The table therefore distinguishes filling all seats from maximizing ticket revenue.

topics.title: Two passenger types and two fares
topics.body:
The lecture separates business travelers who purchase within 14 days of departure from leisure travelers who purchase at least 15 days ahead. Its observed business/leisure counts are 52/3 at $40, 40/0 at $50, 65/37 at $30 and 57/8 at $38. The last row's type counts disagree with its printed total, as noted below.
The displayed fitted curves are q₁ = 90 − p₁ and q₂ = 160 − 4p₂. Restricting expected passenger counts to be nonnegative gives:
$$q_1(p_1)=\max(0,90-p_1),\qquad q_2(p_2)=\max(0,160-4p_2).$$
Under one fare, these demands add to the piecewise total-demand curve. For two fares, the two segment revenues share the 130-seat capacity.

sections.title: Derive the lecture's two-fare result
sections.body:
Ignoring capacity initially, business revenue is p₁(90 − p₁), maximized at p₁ = 45 with q₁ = 45. Leisure revenue is p₂(160 − 4p₂), maximized at p₂ = 20 with q₂ = 80. The total is 125 passengers, so the capacity constraint does not change these separate maxima.
$$R=45(45)+20(80)=3625.$$
This reproduces strategy 4 in the lecture's comparison table. It assumes that the booking restrictions separate the customer types. Allowing every passenger to buy the lower fare would require a different demand model.

topics.warning: The observed-data table on Chapter 1 page 26 has an internal inconsistency at fare $38: total tickets are listed as 60, but the type counts 57 and 8 add to 65. These entries are preserved as printed; the worked pricing calculations use the fitted curves supplied in the lecture.

topics.title: App specials and a binding seat constraint
topics.body:
The lecture's final comparison keeps 30 full-fare business passengers paying $60 while an app special attracts additional price-sensitive business travelers. Its strategy 5 result is app fare $40 with 20 app users; strategy 6 reports app fare $32 with 28 app users and leisure fare $22 with 72 leisure users.
The following is a worked reconstruction of those results from the displayed demand curves. At app fare a, total business demand on q₁ = 90 − a is split into 30 full-fare customers and residual app demand 60 − a. Leisure demand at fare b is 160 − 4b. Use 0 ≤ a ≤ 60 and 0 ≤ b ≤ 40:
$$R=1800+a(60-a)+b(160-4b).$$
$$30+(60-a)+(160-4b)\le130\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad a+4b\ge120.$$
This reconstruction assumes that the 30 full-fare passengers do not switch to the app. The slides' final table is consistent with that assumption, but the formula is an explanatory derivation rather than an explicitly printed app-demand equation.

sections.title: Strategy 5: leisure fare fixed at $20
sections.body:
At the fixed leisure fare there are 80 leisure passengers and 30 full-fare passengers, leaving 20 seats for the app. Capacity requires a ≥ 40. App revenue a(60 − a) decreases above its unconstrained maximum at a = 30, so choose a = 40. Revenue is 1,800 + 40×20 + 20×80 = $4,200, matching the comparison table.
Before adding the app special, the $60/$20 pair on page 30 sells 110 tickets and gives calculated revenue $3,400.

sections.title: Strategy 6: app and leisure fares both variable
sections.body:
The unconstrained choices a = 30 and b = 20 would demand 140 seats, so the capacity constraint binds at the maximum. Substitute a = 120 − 4b:
$$R(b)=-5400+880b-20b^2.$$
The resulting concave quadratic is maximized at b = 22 and a = 32. Counts are 30 full-fare, 28 app and 72 leisure passengers, filling exactly 130 seats. Revenue is 1,800 + 896 + 1,584 = $4,280, reproducing strategy 6 in the lecture table.

topics.title: Methods and decision support systems
topics.body:
Linear programming uses a clear objective, resource restrictions and known parameters. Probabilistic methods explicitly represent uncertainty. Network methods express relationships as nodes and connections and may be deterministic or probabilistic. Forecasting, inventory models, simulation and multicriteria methods address other structures.
Applications in the slides include scheduling, production planning, inventory, pricing, product assortment, capital budgeting, delivery routes and satellite scheduling. The INFORMS journals on applied analytics and data science provide examples of implementation.
A decision support system combines a user interface, databases and management-science models. The decision maker asks “what if?”, compares alternatives and examines sensitivity. ERP systems illustrate how these tools connect across organizational functions and internet-based operations.

topics.title: Case study: making scheduling results usable
topics.body:
The Mitsubishi production-scheduling example illustrates that a solution also needs a usable interface. The old tool needed about two hours to draw 100,000 schedule items, around 13 items per second. Users also needed to move and resize bars, change colors and hatching, show labels and tooltips, change the time scale, open nested rows and resize columns.
The targets were 20,000 items within 10–20 seconds and 100,000 within 0.1–0.2 hour. Instead of preparing the entire chart before displaying anything, compute and draw the requested portion immediately.
A block is a group of schedule data; the view is the visible region; an extended view caches surrounding content. When the view changes, refresh the screen and cache as needed. Modifications update the local scheduling cache and then the database. The interface, drawing/data-management layer and cache separate presentation from server storage.

sections.title: Reported evaluation and its historical setup
sections.body:
The stated development target on page 50 used a Core 2 Duo E6550 2.33 GHz PC, 2 GB RAM and Windows XP. The prototype evaluation on page 54 used a different configuration: a Core 2 Duo P8700 2.53 GHz PC, 4 GB RAM, Windows 7 SP1 and SQL Server 2008. The implementation was in VB.NET.
Five tests were run in each size group. Group A contained about 2,000 rows and 20,000 items, with mean time 17.6 seconds and peak memory below 100 MB. Group B contained about 10,000 rows and 100,000 items, with mean time 131 seconds and peak memory below 200 MB.
The slides report approximately 763 items per second and about 60 times the old tool's throughput. These are historical evaluation results with the stated data and hardware, not a current cross-platform benchmark. The implementation lesson is to compute and draw the requested portion of the schedule rather than delay the interface until the whole chart is prepared.

title: Formulate and solve a linear program
subtitle: Chapter 2 · Geometry
outcomes: Build resource, requirement and mixture constraints.
Read a feasible region and distinguish optimal, infeasible and unbounded models.

topics.title: The four assumptions of linear programming
topics.body:
An LP consists of decision variables, a linear objective, linear constraints and variable bounds. The coefficients and right-hand-side values are parameters. To apply it, identify the decision, formulate the model, solve it and implement the result.
Proportionality means a coefficient stays constant as the activity level changes. Additivity means contributions combine by addition, without interaction terms. Divisibility allows fractional variable values. Certainty treats the model’s inputs as known.
$$\max\; c^Tx\quad\text{subject to }Ax\le b,\;x\ge0.$$
This compact form is an example, not a restriction: an LP can minimize, include equalities or lower-bound requirements, and have other variable bounds. Products of decision variables, squared variables and variable denominators are not linear.
For every variable, state its unit and time period. Every term in one constraint must have the same unit. If actual choices must be whole numbers, an integer model may be required; rounding an LP solution can break feasibility.

check.question: Which expression is linear in x and y?
check.explanation: Coefficients may be constants, but products and powers of decision variables are not linear.

topics.title: Beaver Creek: bowls and mugs
topics.body:
Let x₁ be bowls per day and x₂ mugs per day. Each bowl earns $40, uses one labor hour and 4 lb of clay. Each mug earns $50, uses two hours and 3 lb of clay. There are 40 labor hours and 120 lb of clay available per day.
$$\max Z=40x_1+50x_2$$
$$x_1+2x_2\le40,\qquad4x_1+3x_2\le120,\qquad x_1,x_2\ge0.$$
At (5,10), labor use is 25 and clay use is 50: 4×5 + 3×10 = 50 lb. Both limits are satisfied and profit is $700. The slides print 70 for that clay sum; the correct total is 50.
At (10,20), labor use is 50, exceeding 40, so the plan is infeasible even though its nominal profit is $1,400. Feasibility requires every constraint, including bounds, to hold.

sections.title: Slack and binding constraints
sections.body: For an upper-bound resource, slack equals availability minus usage. At (5,10), labor slack is 15 and clay slack is 70. A constraint binds when slack is zero. A feasible plan need not be optimal, and a high objective value does not rescue an infeasible plan.

topics.warning: The visible product data and handwritten model on Chapter 2 Part 2 pages 6–8 use 4x₁ + 3x₂ ≤ 120. Some later printed repetitions, including pages 12, 13, 16 and 18, instead show 4x₂ + 3x₂. Page 12 also prints 4×5 + 3×10 = 70, although the arithmetic equals 50. Calculations and redrawn graphs here use the product data and the handwritten correct model.

topics.title: Graphical solution and corner points
topics.body:
For two variables, draw each constraint boundary, select the permitted half-plane and intersect all the restrictions with the variable bounds. The pottery slide illustrates the resource lines and feasible region. For a ≤ resource constraint, the origin is often a useful test point; a ≥ requirement can select the opposite side.
Worked calculation from the slide model: the pottery feasible vertices are (0,0), (0,20), (24,8) and (30,0). Their objective values are $0, $1,000, $1,360 and $1,200, respectively. Thus the best plan is 24 bowls and 8 mugs. The redrawn feasible-region diagram and interactive controls use these equations rather than treating imprecise hand-drawn axes as numerical measurements.

sections.title: Worked derivation of the binding intersection
sections.body:
$$x_1+2x_2=40,\qquad4x_1+3x_2=120.$$
Multiply the first equation by four and subtract the second: 5x₂ = 40, hence x₂ = 8 and x₁ = 24. Both resources are exhausted.
A constant-profit line has slope −c₁/c₂. Translating it toward larger profit identifies the last feasible contact. In this bounded pottery polygon, a finite maximum occurs at a vertex; if an objective is parallel to an edge, every point of that edge can tie.

check.question: At the standard pottery optimum, how much labor remains?

topics.title: Fertilizer: a minimization model
topics.body:
Let x₁ be bags of Super-gro and x₂ bags of Crop-quick. The slide costs are $6 and $3 per bag. Their nitrogen contributions are 2 and 4 lb per bag, and phosphate contributions are 4 and 3 lb per bag. The field needs at least 16 lb nitrogen and 24 lb phosphate:
$$\min Z=6x_1+3x_2$$
$$2x_1+4x_2\ge16,\qquad4x_1+3x_2\ge24,\qquad x_1,x_2\ge0.$$
Working from these constraints, the feasible region extends upward and rightward, with lower-boundary vertices (0,8), (4.8,1.6) and (8,0). Their calculated costs are $24, $33.60 and $48. Buy 8 bags of Crop-quick and no Super-gro. This agrees with the handwritten (0,8), Z = $24 on Part 2 page 15.
At that plan, nitrogen supplied is 32 lb, leaving surplus 16 lb, and phosphate is exactly 24 lb. This example has an unbounded feasible region but a finite minimum cost.
topics.warning: Part 1 page 15 repeats a phosphate-row subscript typo. The ingredient table and Part 2 handwritten model give 4x₁ + 3x₂ ≥ 24, which is the constraint used here.

topics.title: Multiple optima, infeasibility and unboundedness
topics.body:
The slide examples discuss changing unit profits, alternate optima, infeasibility and unboundedness. For the pottery calculations here, retain the product-data constraints x₁ + 2x₂ ≤ 40 and 4x₁ + 3x₂ ≤ 120, with nonnegative variables. This avoids the repeated printed clay-row typo noted in the pottery topic.
Worked evaluation for profits $70 and $20: the vertex profits are 0, 400, 1,840 and 2,100, so (30,0) becomes optimal. The feasible set stays fixed while the objective selects a different vertex.
For the alternate-optimum example, the objective 40x₁ + 30x₂ equals ten times clay usage. Every feasible point on the clay boundary between (24,8) and (30,0) therefore earns $1,200. The diagram is a redraw from those equations; the equality of objective values follows from this calculation.

sections.title: An infeasible model
sections.body:
$$\max Z=5x_1+3x_2,\qquad4x_1+2x_2\le8,\quad x_1\ge4,\quad x_2\ge6.$$
The lower bounds force the left side to be at least 28, contradicting the upper bound 8. Hence the lecture's model has no feasible solution, regardless of its objective.

sections.title: An unbounded objective
sections.body:
$$\max(4x_1+2x_2),\qquad x_1\ge4,\quad0\le x_2\le2.$$
Increasing x₁ indefinitely stays feasible and increases profit without limit. This is an unbounded maximization problem. It often signals an omitted resource restriction, but whether one is missing must be decided from the original problem.

topics.title: Mixture constraints: chicken and beef
topics.body:
The slide specifies a 1,000 lb batch with chicken costing $3/lb and beef costing $5/lb. Requirements are at least 500 lb chicken, at least 200 lb beef, and a chicken-to-beef ratio of at least two to one.
Worked formulation from those stated data: let c and b be pounds of chicken and beef.
$$\min Z=3c+5b,\quad c+b=1000,\quad c\ge500,\quad b\ge200,\quad c\ge2b.$$
Substitute c = 1,000 − b. The constraints give 200 ≤ b ≤ 1,000/3, and cost becomes 3,000 + 2b. The derived minimum uses b = 200 and c = 800, at cost $3,400.
Because total batch weight is an equality, the feasible mixtures form a line segment. Writing the ratio as c ≥ 2b keeps the formulation linear. The formulation, numerical answer and native graph here are worked additions based on the slide's ingredient requirements.

topics.title: Furniture production and a second graph
topics.body:
Let x₁ be doors and x₂ windows. Workshop 1 allows four door-hours, workshop 2 allows 12 hours with two per window, and workshop 3 allows 18 hours with three per door and two per window. Profit is $300 per door and $500 per window.
$$\max Z=300x_1+500x_2,\quad x_1\le4,\quad2x_2\le12,\quad3x_1+2x_2\le18,\quad x\ge0.$$
The vertices are (0,0), (4,0), (4,3), (2,6), (0,6). Profits are 0, 1,200, 2,700, 3,600 and 3,000. The optimal mix is two doors and six windows, using all hours in workshops 2 and 3, and leaving two hours in workshop 1.

sections.title: Worked solution of the final graphical exercise
sections.body:
The exercise appears on Part 1 page 27 and Part 2 page 24:
$$\max Z=4x_1+5x_2,\quad x_1+2x_2\le10,\quad6x_1+6x_2\le36,\quad x_1\le4,\quad x_1,x_2\ge0.$$
Divide the second constraint by six. Calculating the intersections gives vertices (0,0), (4,0), (4,2), (2,4) and (0,5), with objective values 0, 16, 26, 28 and 25. Thus the derived optimum is (2,4), Z = 28. The x₁ upper bound has slack 2.

title: What changes the best decision?
subtitle: Chapter 2 · Sensitivity
outcomes: Find objective-coefficient ranges and local shadow prices.
Distinguish changes in prices, resources and technology.

topics.title: Changing objective coefficients
topics.body:
The slides pose coefficient-range exercises for the pottery graph. The ranges below are worked derivations from that graph, using its intended clay row 4x₁ + 3x₂ ≤ 120.
Objective sensitivity asks how much a coefficient can change while the current optimal point remains optimal. For the pottery intersection (24,8), the objective slope must lie between the slopes of its two adjacent edges, −1/2 and −4/3.
$$\frac12\le\frac{c_1}{c_2}\le\frac43\quad(c_2>0).$$
Hold c₂ = 50: 25 ≤ c₁ ≤ 200/3 ≈ 66.67. Hold c₁ = 40: 30 ≤ c₂ ≤ 80. At either endpoint the current point is still optimal, but an adjacent edge also becomes optimal. These are one-at-a-time ranges; they cannot be applied independently to simultaneous coefficient changes.

sections.title: Derived algebra for the lecture exercise
sections.body:
Slide 30 contains the algebra-exercise heading but no displayed working. The following derives the result from the two resource rows.
The value of one labor hour is yL and one pound of clay is yC. With both pottery products produced, their profits equal the imputed resource costs:
$$y_L+4y_C=c_1,\quad2y_L+3y_C=c_2.$$
$$y_L=\frac{4c_2-3c_1}{5},\qquad y_C=\frac{2c_1-c_2}{5}.$$
Requiring both values to be nonnegative gives the same objective-coefficient range. At the original profits, yL = 16 and yC = 6.

topics.warning: Slides 25–27 print 4x₂ + 3x₂ ≤ 120 in the model block, while their graph labels the clay line 4x₁ + 3x₂ = 120. This reader uses the graph-consistent clay row, also supported by the input table and later slides.

topics.title: Cost sensitivity and reduced cost
topics.body:
The lecture supplies the fertilizer graph and poses the two coefficient-range questions. The endpoint analysis and reduced-cost interpretation below are worked derivations; the numerical reduced cost is also shown in the Chapter 3 sensitivity report.
At the fertilizer optimum (0,8), the adjacent edge toward (4.8,1.6) has slope −4/3. The point remains optimal when c₂ ≥ 0 and c₁ ≥ (4/3)c₂. Holding c₂ = 3 gives c₁ ≥ 4. Holding c₁ = 6 gives 0 ≤ c₂ ≤ 4.5.
At c₁ = 4 or c₂ = 4.5, a whole boundary edge has the same cost. At c₂ = 0 and c₁ positive, any feasible point with x₁ = 0 has zero cost. If c₂ becomes negative, buying arbitrarily many Crop-quick bags makes this unbounded minimization model decrease without limit.
Reduced cost measures the objective penalty of bringing a currently zero variable into the solution, under the current optimal basis. For Super-gro, one bag costs $6 but replaces $4 of Crop-quick when phosphate remains binding. Its reduced cost is 2, and its cost must fall by $2 before it can enter without worsening the objective.

topics.title: Labor availability and shadow price
topics.body:
The slides ask for the effect of labor changing from 40 to 60, from 40 to 30, and locally around 40. The following works these questions from the stated model.
An RHS sensitivity range preserves the optimal basis, not the numerical values of the decision variables. With pottery clay fixed at 120 lb and labor availability L, solve the same two binding constraints:
$$x_1=48-0.6L,\qquad x_2=0.8L-24.$$
Both variables remain nonnegative for 30 ≤ L ≤ 80. Within this range:
$$Z^*(L)=720+16L.$$
The shadow price is $16 per additional labor hour. From 40 to 60 hours, profit rises by 20×16 = $320 to $1,680, with (12,24). At 30 hours, profit is $1,200 with (30,0). This marginal value is local; it is not a purchase recommendation without considering the cost of acquiring more labor.

sections.title: Derived full value function
sections.body:
$$Z^*(L)=\begin{cases}40L&0\le L\le30\\720+16L&30\le L\le80\\2000&L\ge80.\end{cases}$$
For scarce labor, make only bowls because they earn more per labor hour. Above 80 hours, clay limits production to 40 mugs and extra labor has no value. The successive marginal values are 40, 16 and 0; at the breakpoints the left and right derivatives differ.

check.question: Does the current mix (24,8) stay numerically unchanged when labor increases to 41 hours?
options: No: the basis stays, but quantities change
check.explanation: The new quantities are 23.4 bowls and 8.8 mugs. Profit rises by $16.

topics.warning: Slide 32 describes an unchanged “solution variable mix” and groups different positive quantities together. Here this means retaining the current basis/product pattern, not retaining the numerical quantities (24,8). At a range endpoint a basic variable can become zero.

topics.title: Clay availability and the value of a resource
topics.body:
This is a worked solution to the lecture’s clay-availability questions, derived with the original labor limit fixed at 40 hours.
Keep labor at 40 hours and let clay availability be C. At the intersection:
$$x_1=\frac{2C-120}{5},\qquad x_2=\frac{160-C}{5}.$$
The basis remains feasible for 60 ≤ C ≤ 160, and optimal profit is 640 + 6C. Thus the shadow price at C = 120 is $6 per pound. Reducing clay to 80 lowers profit by $240 to $1,120; the new mix is (8,16).

sections.title: Derived values beyond the local range
sections.body:
$$Z^*(C)=\begin{cases}\frac{50}{3}C&0\le C\le60\\640+6C&60\le C\le160\\1600&C\ge160.\end{cases}$$
With little clay, mugs earn more per pound of clay. With abundant clay, labor limits production to 40 bowls. The successive marginal values are 50/3, 6 and 0 dollars per pound.

topics.title: Requirement sensitivity in a minimum-cost model
topics.body:
The lecture asks how shadow prices change as each nutrient requirement varies. The formula below is derived from its stated fertilizer model; Chapter 3 also shows the original-point sensitivity report.
A higher nutrient minimum can raise the least achievable cost. At the current fertilizer solution, nitrogen is already oversupplied; its shadow price is zero. Phosphate binds and its shadow price is $1 per additional pound.
Crop-quick is cheaper per pound of both nutrients. For any nonnegative nitrogen requirement N and phosphate requirement P, the optimal solution uses only Crop-quick:
$$x_1^*=0,\quad x_2^*=\max\left(\frac N4,\frac P3\right),\quad Z^*=\max\left(\frac{3N}{4},P\right).$$
Hold P = 24. Cost stays 24 until N reaches 32, then rises at $0.75 per pound of required nitrogen. Hold N = 16. Cost stays 12 until P reaches 12, then rises at $1 per pound of required phosphate. At N = 16, P = 24, nitrogen can increase by 16 before its shadow price changes; phosphate can decrease by 12 before its current shadow price changes.
For nonnegative requirements, the current nitrogen range is 0–32 and the phosphate range is 12 upward. A solver can report an effectively infinite allowable decrease for a redundant nitrogen lower bound; negative nutrient requirements have no physical meaning here.

topics.title: A new product and a second factory
topics.body:
Slide 40 supplies the new cup’s data and augmented LP. The shadow-price test and threshold below are derived from that model.
A cup would earn $30, using 1.2 labor hours and 2 lb of clay. At the current shadow prices its resources are worth 1.2×16 + 2×6 = $31.20. Its net contribution relative to these scarce resources is −$1.20, so adding it cannot improve the original optimum.
$$\max40x_1+50x_2+30x_3$$
$$x_1+2x_2+1.2x_3\le40,\qquad4x_1+3x_2+2x_3\le120,\quad x\ge0.$$
At profit 31.20, producing some cups can become an alternate optimum; above that threshold re-solve the model. The shadow-price test is based on the current model and its resource tradeoffs.

sections.title: Willow Valley: model and derived comparison
sections.body:
The second-factory image on slide 39 uses profits 48 and 60, labor coefficients 2 and 3, and clay coefficients 4 and 3. Write its overwritten labor availability as H:
$$\max Z_W=48y_1+60y_2;\quad2y_1+3y_2\le H,\quad4y_1+3y_2\le120,\quad y_1,y_2\ge0.$$
The following is a derived solution for H ≥ 0, not a numerical result printed on the slide. For 0 ≤ H ≤ 60, produce (y₁,y₂) = (H/2,0). For 60 ≤ H ≤ 120, both resource rows bind, giving y₁ = (120 − H)/2 and y₂ = (2H − 120)/3. For H ≥ 120, produce (0,40).
$$Z_W^*(H)=\begin{cases}24H&0\le H\le60\\480+16H&60\le H\le120\\2400&H\ge120.\end{cases}$$
In the interior range 60 < H < 120, Willow’s labor shadow price is 16 and its clay shadow price is 4. At H = 40, the optimum is (20,0), Z = 960. At H = 65, the optimum is (27.5,10/3), Z = 1,520. These are alternative parameter examples, not two simultaneous labor limits. Compare resource values under the same stated availability rather than comparing unit profits alone.

topics.warning: The labor RHS in the source image is overwritten in red; the red correction appears to read 65. This reader retains the parameter H and explicitly labels the two illustrative RHS values. The visible coefficient before y₁ is 2; using 1 would describe a different factory.

topics.title: Furniture sensitivity and changing technology
topics.body:
The lecture gives the furniture model and asks about door-profit sensitivity and Workshop 3’s shadow price. The ranges and value calculations below are derived answers to those questions.
For the furniture solution (2,6), hold the window profit at 500. Door profit can range from 0 to 750 while that point remains optimal. At zero, producing fewer doors is equally good; at 750, the workshop-3 boundary edge becomes equally profitable.
Let workshop 3 have H hours. Between 12 and 24 hours, windows remain 6 and doors are (H − 12)/3. The profit is 1,800 + 100H, so workshop 3 has a shadow price of $100 per hour. Its original 18 hours can decrease by 6 or increase by 6 within this basis.
For H below 12, only windows are made and the marginal value is $250 per hour; above 24, workshops 1 and 2 cap output at (4,6), so extra workshop-3 time has zero value.

sections.title: Constraint-coefficient change: slide illustration and exact calculation
sections.body:
If pottery labor per bowl changes from 1 to α, the labor boundary is αx₁ + 2x₂ ≤ 40. This rotates the line rather than shifting it in parallel. Objective and RHS sensitivity ranges do not answer this change directly.
The slides illustrate α ≈ 1.33 and label the bowl-only point (30,0). At α = 4/3 exactly, the solution is (30,0), Z = 1,200. If 1.33 is interpreted literally, the intersection is approximately (29.9252,0.0998), with Z ≈ 1,201.995. Preserve the distinction between a rounded coefficient and its exact value. The exact and literal-decimal solutions here are calculated from the model; the slide displays only the rounded bowl-only result.

title: From a model to a solver
subtitle: Chapter 3
outcomes: Build spreadsheet and COPT models, inspect the loaded formulation, and read solver results.
Use LP/MPS files, command scripts and the Python API; interpret sensitivity and benchmarks critically.

topics.title: Build the pottery model in Excel
topics.body:
Computer solvers automate procedures such as the simplex method. The slides introduce Excel Solver and Cardinal Optimizer (COPT), alongside examples of other optimization packages. Software solves the formulation supplied to it; it cannot check whether the coefficients express the intended business problem.
Separate inputs, decision cells, objective and constraint calculations. In the slide spreadsheet, C2:D2 contains profits 40 and 50; C3:D3 labor coefficients 1 and 2; C4:D4 clay coefficients 4 and 3. C6 contains 40 and C7 contains 120. C11:D11 holds the changing production quantities.
Set C15 to =SUMPRODUCT(C11:D11,C2:D2), C19 to =SUMPRODUCT(C3:D3,C11:D11), and C20 to =SUMPRODUCT(C4:D4,C11:D11). E19 links to C6 and E20 to C7.
In the demonstrated Solver setup, maximize C15 by changing C11:D11, subject to C19:C20 ≤ E19:E20. Apply nonnegative bounds and use the Simplex LP method. Solve, then independently substitute the returned values into every original constraint.
The expected result is (24,8), profit 1,360, labor usage 40 and clay usage 120. The Answer Report marks both resource constraints binding with zero slack. The original values shown in a report are the initial guesses, not a second optimum.
topics.warning: The model block at the left of slides 4–5 repeats the clay-row typo 4x₂ + 3x₂. The visible spreadsheet instead uses coefficients 4 and 3 under bowl and mug, and its Solver report returns (24,8), Z = 1,360. The formulas here follow that spreadsheet.

topics.title: Read sensitivity reports without overextending them
topics.body:
An objective-coefficient range is current coefficient minus allowable decrease through current coefficient plus allowable increase. For pottery bowls, 40 − 15 = 25 and 40 + 26.6667 = 66.6667. For mugs, 50 − 20 = 30 and 50 + 30 = 80. Both produced variables have reduced cost zero.
The labor report gives RHS 40, shadow price 16, allowable decrease 10 and increase 40: range 30–80. Clay gives RHS 120, shadow price 6, decrease 60 and increase 40: range 60–160. Within an RHS range, the optimal quantities can change even though the basis is retained; “unchanged solution variable mix” in the slide is not unchanged numerical quantities.
For fertilizer, the changing cells are C9:C10. Minimize C13 = SUMPRODUCT(C2:C3,C9:C10). The nutrient left sides are SUMPRODUCT(C9:C10,D2:D3) and SUMPRODUCT(C9:C10,E2:E3), each constrained above its requirement. The answer is (0,8), total cost 24.
The fertilizer report gives Super-gro reduced cost 2, cost coefficient 6 and allowable decrease 2; Crop-quick coefficient 3, increase 1.5 and decrease 3. Nitrogen’s shadow price is 0 with surplus 16; phosphate’s is 1. Large entries such as 1E+30 denote an effectively unbounded allowable change in the software’s reporting convention.
One-at-a-time sensitivity reports are local and conditional. Integer restrictions, changed coefficients in the constraint matrix or simultaneous data changes can require solving again.

topics.title: Aircraft parts: verify a numerical solution
topics.body:
Let x₁ and x₂ be production quantities of the two aircraft parts. The three stages are stamping, drilling and finishing.
$$\max Z=650x_1+910x_2$$
$$4x_1+7.5x_2\le105,\quad6.2x_1+4.9x_2\le90,\quad9.1x_1+4.1x_2\le110,\quad x\ge0.$$
Derived continuous-LP solution (the slide supplies the model, not these calculated results): solving the first two boundaries gives x₁ ≈ 5.96654 and x₂ ≈ 10.81784. Profit is approximately $13,722.49. Finishing usage is about 98.64870 hours, leaving about 11.35130 hours. Thus stamping and drilling bind while finishing does not.
These are continuous LP quantities. If the decision requires whole aircraft parts, impose integrality and solve the resulting integer model; independently rounding the displayed solution is not justified by this lecture’s LP calculation.

topics.title: Read a solver benchmark critically
topics.body:
The revised Chapter 3 adds a dated solver comparison and a case study about how benchmark selection affects a claim. A benchmark measures particular solver versions on a specified instance set, hardware and stopping rule. It does not establish a universal ordering for every optimization problem.
The LPopt snapshot is dated April 29, 2026 and concerns finding an optimal basic solution on 65 instances. It reports COPT 8.0.0 with score 1.00 and 100% solved. The virtual-best entry is an ensemble reference that selects the best observed solver per instance, rather than a separate solver available for an individual run. Treat this table as the course's historical example, not a current product recommendation.
The slide history contrasts the complete 240-instance MIPLIB2017 benchmark set with an advertised comparison on 99 selected instances. A selected subset can change measured ratios and need not represent the full benchmark. The slides reproduce a 2018 retraction and describe later benchmark withdrawals. These are source context for evaluating evidence, not proof that one solver will perform best on your model.
When reading a comparison, check the exact instance list, solver versions, machine and thread settings, time limits, aggregation rule and treatment of unsolved instances. Read the solved fraction alongside the aggregate score. Test candidate solvers on representative models of your own before drawing a decision-specific conclusion.

topics.title: LP files and the COPT command-line workflow
topics.body:
The Chapter 3 screenshots use COPT 7.2. The separate September 29 tutorial demonstrates COPT 8.0.7 and a corrected pottery model. Both workflows read a formulation, solve it and export the result. The tutorial introduces programming interfaces as well as the interactive shell and modeling-tool connectors.
Start the interactive shell with copt_cmd. Use pwd to check its working directory, cd to change directories, and dir or ls to list available model files. If a path contains spaces, quote it. A shell can only read a file from a path it can find.
Use read pottery.lp to load the corrected model below, then opt to solve it and writesol pottery.sol to save the result. An optimal result gives x₁ = 24, x₂ = 8 and Z = 1,360. Both constraints bind. Substituting the values gives labor 24 + 2(8) = 40 and clay 4(24) + 3(8) = 120.
The course also shows set timelimit 10, writeparam, display/get, optlp, iis, feasrelax, tune and loadtuneparam. Commands and available attributes depend on the installed version. The tutorial points to the copt80 manual in its example installation, while the older Chapter 3 screenshots point to copt72.
An IIS identifies a set of conflicting constraints. Feasibility relaxation changes bounds or constraints to make a problem solvable. Neither operation establishes that a changed formulation still represents the original business requirements. Always inspect solver status before reporting objective values or variable values.
topics.warning: The older Chapter 3 screenshots still use 4x₂ + 3x₂ ≤ 120 and return (40,0), Z = 1,600. That solves the mistyped model. The separate COPT tutorial corrects the row to 4x₁ + 3x₂ ≤ 120 and reports (24,8), Z = 1,360.

topics.title: Write LP files without changing the model
topics.body:
An LP file is a plain-text optimization model. Maximize or Minimize introduces the objective, Subject To introduces constraints, and Bounds specifies variable bounds. End terminates the file. Use unique constraint names and ordinary comparison operators such as <= and >=.
Variables are continuous and nonnegative unless declared otherwise. A free variable needs an explicit free bound. Generals declares integer variables and Binaries declares variables restricted to zero or one. Those declarations change the mathematical problem. The tutorial's small format example includes both an integer and a binary variable, so it is a mixed-integer example even though the lecture section discusses LP files.
On Windows, show file-name extensions before renaming a text document. A file named example.lp.txt is still a text document with a hidden .txt suffix. Use a plain-text editor and separate numeric coefficients from variable names.
The tutorial's parsing example shows why syntax checking alone is insufficient: 4x2 can be read as a variable name rather than four times x2. Its particular malformed file also treats 32 as a variable and combines repeated coefficients on that variable. This is an observed parser trap in the demonstrated file, not a safe way to express a numeric constant.
Export the model and compare its rows and columns with the intended algebra before solving. An MPS export can expose unexpected names and merged coefficients, but changing file format cannot repair an incorrect model on its own.

code.title: Correct pottery.lp
code.body:
Maximize
  profit: 40 x1 + 50 x2
Subject To
  labor: x1 + 2 x2 <= 40
  clay: 4 x1 + 3 x2 <= 120
Bounds
  x1 >= 0
  x2 >= 0
End

tables.caption: LP sections and what they declare
rows: Lower/upper bounds; e.g. x1 free permits either sign

check.question: You intend the coefficient 4 times x2 in a plain-text LP file. Which form avoids the demonstrated token trap?
check.explanation: Separate the coefficient and variable name with a space. The course example shows that an attached token such as 4x2 can be interpreted as a variable name.

topics.title: Inspect, export and script a COPT solve
topics.body:
After read pottery.lp, inspect the model before accepting any solve. The corrected pottery formulation has two constraint rows, two variables and four nonzero coefficients in its constraint matrix. Bounds are separate from those two algebraic rows. A column count greater than expected can reveal that a malformed numeric token became a variable.
The tutorial demonstrates get rows, get cols, get objsense and get elems. It also inspects maxelem, minelem, maxrhs and minrhs. These report model dimensions, objective sense and coefficient or bound magnitudes. Very different magnitudes can motivate checking units and scaling, but an attribute report is not a proof of correctness.
Use writelp pottery-check.lp or writemps pottery.mps to export the loaded model. LP emphasizes human-readable algebra. MPS records named rows and variable-by-variable coefficients. Its ROWS codes N, L, G and E denote the objective, <=, >= and equality rows; COLUMNS holds nonzero coefficients; RHS holds row constants; ENDATA terminates the model. Inspect names and coefficients in either export instead of relying on the original input text alone.
The tutorial contrasts output ordering and parsing behavior of its LP and MPS exports. Those observations describe the demonstrated tools and files; file layout should not be treated as a mathematical property or a universal guarantee for every reader and writer.
After an optimal solve, writesol pottery.sol exports objective and variable values. Exporting LP/MPS does not optimize the problem, while writing a solution file does not establish that the business model was formulated correctly.
For repeatable runs, put commands in an .in file and execute load pottery.in from the COPT shell. The script below adapts the tutorial’s example to the pottery filenames: load the model, set a 10-second limit, solve, then write the solution. A time limit can stop a different problem before optimality, so inspect the final status rather than assuming that every script run found an optimum.

tables.caption: Useful model attributes from the tutorial
rows: Nonzero entries of the constraint matrix

code.title: pottery.in
code.body:
read pottery.lp
set timelimit 10
opt
writesol pottery.sol

topics.title: Build the same model with the COPT Python API
topics.body:
The tutorial also constructs the pottery model directly in Python. It installs the interface with pip install coptpy and refers students to the full COPT setup instructions on Learn. A package installation and the solver's licensing/setup requirements are separate steps.
Create an environment and model, add nonnegative variables, add both resource constraints, set the maximizing objective, choose any parameters and solve. Model construction through expressions avoids manually spelling coefficient-variable tokens in an LP text file.
Check model.status == COPT.OPTIMAL before using the result as an optimum. For the corrected continuous pottery LP, the script returns x1 = 24, x2 = 8 and objective 1,360. Both variable reduced costs are zero, while the labor and clay dual values are 16 and 6. These reproduce the lecture's local shadow prices for this continuous LP and its current basis.
The runnable example below follows tutorial slide 11 and names the constraints for readable output. The extra explicit non-optimal-status error is an author addition. Reduced costs and row duals need the appropriate continuous LP solution; do not reinterpret them automatically as sensitivity reports for an integer model.

code.title: Complete pottery example (requires coptpy)
code.body:
"""Pottery LP from the COPT course tutorial. Requires coptpy."""
import coptpy as cp
from coptpy import COPT

env = cp.Envr()
model = env.createModel("pottery")
x1 = model.addVar(lb=0, name="x1")
x2 = model.addVar(lb=0, name="x2")
model.addConstr(x1 + 2*x2 <= 40, name="labor")
model.addConstr(4*x1 + 3*x2 <= 120, name="clay")
model.setObjective(40*x1 + 50*x2, sense=COPT.MAXIMIZE)
model.setParam(COPT.Param.TimeLimit, 10.0)
model.solve()
if model.status != COPT.OPTIMAL:
    raise RuntimeError(f"No optimal solution: status {model.status}")
print(f"Objective: {model.objval:g}")
for var in model.getVars():
    print(f"{var.name}: value={var.x:g}, reduced_cost={var.RC:g}")
for con in model.getConstrs():
    print(f"{con.name}: dual={con.pi:g}")

title: A toolkit of modeling patterns
subtitle: Chapter 4
outcomes: Formulate product mix, diet, allocation, transport and blending models.
Track inventory, investment timing and relative efficiency.

topics.title: Product mix: printed shirts
topics.body: Quick-Screen produces front-only and front-and-back printed T-shirts and sweatshirts. The visible data give 500 dozen blank garments of each type, $25,000 for production, 72 processing hours, and one truck with room for 1,200 standard boxes. A standard box holds twelve T-shirts; a sweatshirt box holds twelve sweatshirts but occupies three standard-box spaces. The table gives time, production cost and profit per dozen. The question is how many dozens of each product to make to maximize profit.

sections.title: Derived formulation from the slide data
sections.body:
Let x1,x2 be dozens of front-only and front-and-back sweatshirts, and x3,x4 the corresponding T-shirt quantities. The following is a continuous LP derived from the visible data.
$$\max Z=90x_1+125x_2+45x_3+65x_4.$$
$$0.10x_1+0.25x_2+0.08x_3+0.21x_4\le72$$
$$3x_1+3x_2+x_3+x_4\le1200$$
$$36x_1+48x_2+25x_3+35x_4\le25000$$
$$x_1+x_2\le500,\qquad x_3+x_4\le500,\qquad x_i\ge0.$$
The constraints represent processing hours, one truck’s capacity, production budget, sweatshirt stock and T-shirt stock. Profit and cost are separate coefficients: maximize the stated profit, while production cost consumes budget. Do not subtract the cost a second time from an already net profit.

topics.warning: Page 5 visibly provides only model-construction headings. The equations here are the reader’s derivation from the visible data on pages 3-4, not a transcription of a completed lecture formulation.

topics.title: Diet: lower and upper nutrient limits
topics.body: The breakfast table lists ten foods and their nutrients and costs per stated serving: cup, egg, slice or orange. The lecture asks for minimum cost with at least 420 calories, 5 mg iron, 400 mg calcium, 20 g protein and 12 g fiber, and at most 20 g fat and 30 mg cholesterol. The complete table below is transcribed from visible page 6.

sections.title: Derived continuous-serving model
sections.body:
Let xᵢ be servings of food i in the table, using its stated unit (cup, egg, slice or orange). This reader uses a continuous LP, allowing fractional servings; the visible slide does not add whole-serving restrictions. Minimize total cost subject to minimum calories, iron, calcium, protein and fiber, and maximum fat and cholesterol.
$$\min\sum_{i=1}^{10}c_ix_i,\qquad x_i\ge0.$$
Using the table’s nutrient coefficients, require calories ≥ 420, iron ≥ 5 mg, calcium ≥ 400 mg, protein ≥ 20 g, fiber ≥ 12 g, fat ≤ 20 g and cholesterol ≤ 30 mg.
For example, the calorie constraint starts 90x₁ + 110x₂ + 100x₃ + 90x₄ + 75x₅ and continues with the remaining five table entries. The cholesterol constraint is 270x₅ + 8x₆ + 12x₈ ≤ 30; zero coefficients can be omitted. The objective uses the last column, starting 0.18x₁ + 0.22x₂ + 0.10x₃.
Each nutrient gets its own row and direction. A low-cost food can be unattractive because it consumes a limited upper-bound nutrient such as fat or cholesterol.

topics.warning: Page 7 is visibly blank beneath its model-construction headings. Its hidden text layer contains unrelated investment equations, which are not used as diet evidence. The model here is derived from page 6.

topics.title: Investment allocation and ratio restrictions
topics.body: Kathleen Allen has $70,000 to invest for one year. The visible page-8 table gives municipal bonds at 8.5%, CDs at 5%, treasury bills at 6.5% and stock fund at 13%. Municipal bonds may use at most 20% of the total; CDs may not exceed the other three investments combined; CDs and treasury bills together must receive at least 30%; and that group must receive at least 1.2 times the amount in bonds and stock.

sections.title: Derived allocation model
sections.body:
Let x₁, x₂, x₃ and x₄ be dollars in municipal bonds, certificates of deposit, treasury bills and the growth stock fund. Annual returns are 8.5%, 5%, 6.5% and 13%, with total capital $70,000.
$$\max Z=0.085x_1+0.05x_2+0.065x_3+0.13x_4.$$
$$x_1\le14000,\qquad x_2\le x_1+x_3+x_4$$
$$x_2+x_3\ge21000,\qquad x_2+x_3\ge1.2(x_1+x_4)$$
$$x_1+x_2+x_3+x_4=70000,\qquad x_i\ge0.$$
The first restriction caps municipal bonds at 20%. The second limits CDs to the other investments combined. The third puts at least 30% in CDs and treasury bills. The fourth is a ratio restriction comparing the two groups, not “20% of total capital.”
The objective is return earned, not final wealth; adding the fixed initial capital would not change the maximizing allocation. The derived LP uses the listed annual returns as fixed objective coefficients.

topics.warning: The model-summary page 9 is visibly blank beneath its headings. These equations follow from the table on page 8; they are not visible equations from page 9.

topics.title: Marketing: maximize exposure within a budget
topics.body: Biggs Department Store wants to maximize advertising exposure using television, radio and newspaper ads. Visible page 11 gives exposures of 20,000, 12,000 and 9,000 per ad and costs of $15,000, $6,000 and $4,000. Available placements are at most 4 TV commercials, 10 radio commercials and 7 newspaper ads. The agency can produce at most 15 advertisements in total and has a $100,000 budget.

sections.title: Derived LP and the whole-ad distinction
sections.body:
Let x₁, x₂ and x₃ count television commercials, radio commercials and newspaper ads. Exposures are 20,000, 12,000 and 9,000 people per ad; costs are $15,000, $6,000 and $4,000. Budget is $100,000 and production capacity is 15 ads in total.
$$\max Z=20000x_1+12000x_2+9000x_3$$
$$15000x_1+6000x_2+4000x_3\le100000$$
$$x_1\le4,\quad x_2\le10,\quad x_3\le7,\quad x_1+x_2+x_3\le15,\quad x_i\ge0.$$
This reader uses a continuous LP interpretation. The visible model-summary page does not specify an integrality restriction. If ads must be purchased whole, add integer restrictions. The exposure objective is additive as assumed in the data; it does not account for repeated viewers across advertisements.

topics.warning: Page 12 is visibly blank beneath its decision-variable and formulation headings. The LP below is derived from pages 10-11. A requirement to buy whole ads would be an additional integer restriction, not a visible statement in the saved model slide.

topics.title: Transportation: supply, demand and unused capacity
topics.body: Zephyr TV ships televisions monthly from Cincinnati, Atlanta and Pittsburgh to New York, Dallas and Detroit. The visible page-14 table gives supplies 300, 200, 200, demands 150, 250, 200, and lane-specific unit shipping costs. The lecture asks for a minimum-cost shipping plan. Supply totals 700 while stated demand totals 600.

sections.title: Derived model: interpret supply as availability
sections.body:
The visible model page does not explain the 100-unit surplus. For a feasible model of exactly the stated customer demands, this reader treats warehouse supplies as upper bounds and permits unused stock without a modeled cost.
Let xᵢⱼ be televisions shipped from warehouse i to store j. Warehouse supplies are 300 in Cincinnati, 200 in Atlanta and 200 in Pittsburgh. Demands are 150 in New York, 250 in Dallas and 200 in Detroit.
$$\min\sum_i\sum_jc_{ij}x_{ij}.$$
$$\sum_jx_{1j}\le300,\quad\sum_jx_{2j}\le200,\quad\sum_jx_{3j}\le200.$$
$$\sum_ix_{iA}=150,\quad\sum_ix_{iB}=250,\quad\sum_ix_{iC}=200,\quad x_{ij}\ge0.$$
Supply totals 700 and demand totals 600, so 100 units remain at warehouses. If all warehouse rows were forced to equality without an extra destination, the model would be inconsistent. An equivalent balanced formulation adds a dummy destination with demand 100 and zero shipping cost when unused stock has no modeled penalty.
The objective coefficients are lane-specific: choosing the cheapest warehouse separately for every store can violate warehouse capacities. The model coordinates those shared limits.

topics.warning: Page 15 is visibly blank. Warehouse upper bounds and the zero-cost dummy-destination alternative are explicit modeling choices for the 700-versus-600 imbalance; neither choice is displayed on the blank lecture formulation slide.

topics.title: Blending: percentages become linear constraints
topics.body: The petroleum example blends three components into super, premium and extra motor oil. Visible page 17 gives component availability of 4,500, 2,700 and 3,500 barrels/day and purchase costs $12, $10 and $14 per barrel. Grade selling prices are $23, $20 and $18. Each grade must have at least 3,000 barrels. Super needs at least 50% component 1 and at most 30% component 2; premium needs at least 40% component 1 and at most 25% component 3; extra needs at least 60% component 1 and at least 10% component 2.

sections.title: Derived LP formulation
sections.body:
Let xᵢⱼ be barrels of component i used in grade j, with grades S (super), P (premium) and E (extra). Define qⱼ = x₁ⱼ + x₂ⱼ + x₃ⱼ. Component supplies are 4,500, 2,700 and 3,500 barrels/day; costs are $12, $10 and $14 per barrel. Selling prices are 23, 20 and 18 dollars for S, P and E.
$$\max Z=23q_S+20q_P+18q_E-\sum_j(12x_{1j}+10x_{2j}+14x_{3j}).$$
$$\sum_jx_{1j}\le4500,\quad\sum_jx_{2j}\le2700,\quad\sum_jx_{3j}\le3500.$$
$$q_S,q_P,q_E\ge3000,\qquad x_{ij}\ge0.$$
Super needs x₁S ≥ 0.50qS and x₂S ≤ 0.30qS. Premium needs x₁P ≥ 0.40qP and x₃P ≤ 0.25qP. Extra needs x₁E ≥ 0.60qE and x₂E ≥ 0.10qE.
All these restrictions are linear because q is a sum of variables multiplied only by constant percentages. A percentage refers to its own grade’s total, not total company production.
At the minimum 3,000 barrels of each grade, component 1 needs at least 1,500 + 1,200 + 1,800 = 4,500 barrels: its entire supply. Consequently each grade must stay at 3,000 and its component-1 minimum must bind.

sections.title: Derived optimal blend; not a slide answer
sections.body:
Use S = (1,500,900,600), P = (1,200,1,500,300), E = (1,800,300,900), in component order (1,2,3). Totals are 4,500, 2,700 and 1,800. Every grade specification holds. Revenue is 183,000 and ingredient cost is 106,200, leaving profit 76,800.
Because component 1 fixes grade totals and component 2 is cheaper than component 3, using all 2,700 available barrels of component 2 minimizes cost. Other allocations with the same totals and satisfied grade restrictions can have the same optimum.

topics.warning: Page 18 is visibly blank beneath its model-formulation heading. The LP, component-1 argument and $76,800 solution here are reader derivations from the visible page-17 data. The optimal grade totals are fixed, but component allocations can be nonunique.

topics.title: Multiperiod production and inventory
topics.body: PM Computers seeks a production schedule that meets its orders at minimum cost. Visible page 20 gives regular capacity of 160 computers/week, overtime capacity of 50 more per week, unit costs $190 regular and $260 overtime, and holding cost $10/computer/week. Orders in weeks 1-6 are 105, 170, 230, 180, 150 and 250. The saved data page does not state initial or terminal inventory.

sections.title: Derived inventory model and boundary assumptions
sections.body:
Let rₜ, oₜ and Iₜ be regular production, overtime production and ending inventory in week t. For the reader’s model, assume no initial inventory, no backlogs, and no terminal inventory:
$$I_{t-1}+r_t+o_t=d_t+I_t,\qquad I_0=0.$$
$$0\le r_t\le160,\quad0\le o_t\le50,\quad I_t\ge0.$$
$$\min\;190\sum_{t=1}^6r_t+260\sum_{t=1}^6o_t+10\sum_{t=1}^5 I_t.$$
Impose I6 = 0 and charge holding for inventory carried from one week to the next. These boundary and accounting choices complete the model; they are not displayed on the blank source formulation page.
Week 3 demand exceeds that week’s maximum production by 20; week 6 exceeds it by 40. Earlier inventory is essential. Looking only at total six-week capacity would miss these timing constraints.

sections.title: Derived least-cost schedule under these assumptions
sections.body:
Regular production is 160 every week. Use overtime of 0, 0, 25, 20, 30 and 50. Ending inventories are 55, 45, 0, 0, 40 and 0. Check each balance, for example week 3: 45 + 160 + 25 = 230.
Regular production costs 182,400; overtime costs 32,500; holding costs 1,400. Total cost is $216,300. Regular production is cheaper than overtime even with up to five weeks of holding, so all regular capacity is used. The required 125 overtime units are placed as late as the balance and capacity constraints allow.

topics.warning: Page 21 is visibly blank. The $216,300 schedule is a verified reader solution under I0 = I6 = 0, on-time demand with no backlogs, and holding charged between weeks. These boundary assumptions are not visible source facts.

topics.title: Pet food: keep weight and cans consistent
topics.body: Bark’s Pet Food Company produces Meow Chow and Bow Chow from horse meat, fish and cereal. Visible page 23 gives weekly availability of 600 lb horse meat, 800 lb fish and 1,000 lb cereal, plus 2,250 cans holding 16 ounces each. Meow Chow must be at least half fish and Bow Chow at least half horse meat. Stated profits are $0.80 and $0.96 per can. Since 16 ounces equals one pound, ingredient weight and filled-can totals can be matched directly.

sections.title: Derived blending model
sections.body:
Let hM, fM, cM be pounds of the three ingredients in Meow Chow, and hB, fB, cB the amounts in Bow Chow. Define M = hM + fM + cM and B = hB + fB + cB. Because each can is one pound, M and B also count cans.
$$\max Z=0.80M+0.96B$$
$$h_M+h_B\le600,\quad f_M+f_B\le800,\quad c_M+c_B\le1000$$
$$M+B\le2250,\quad f_M\ge0.5M,\quad h_B\ge0.5B,\quad h,f,c\ge0.$$

sections.title: Derived optimal production quantities
sections.body: Horse meat limits B to 1,200. Since Bow Chow has higher profit and both products have positive profit, a best plan uses 1,200 Bow Chow and 1,050 Meow Chow, earning $1,992. One feasible recipe uses 600 horse + 600 cereal for Bow Chow and 650 fish + 400 cereal for Meow Chow. All 2,250 cans are used; 150 lb fish remain.

topics.warning: Page 24 is visibly blank beneath its model-formulation heading. The ingredient-allocation model and $1,992 worked optimum are derived from page 23. The stated per-can profits are used directly.

topics.title: Investment over time: when is money available?
topics.body: The visible page-25 example starts with $100,000 and a five-year horizon. A can start at the beginning of years 1-4 and returns 15% after two years. B starts at the beginning of year 3, pays 25% at the end of year 5, and is capped at $40,000. C starts at the beginning of year 2, pays 40% at the end of year 4, and is capped at $30,000. Government bond D can be purchased at the beginning of each year and gives a 6% return. The question asks how to maximize the return at the end of year 5.

sections.title: Derived cash-flow model with explicit timing conventions
sections.body:
Use thousand-dollar units. Let Aₜ and Dₜ denote amounts invested at the beginning of year t, and B and C the one-time amounts. For this derived flow model, treat each D purchase as a one-year investment returning principal plus 6%, and make maturity proceeds available for reinvestment at the corresponding year boundary. The source says D is bought yearly and returns 6%, but does not explicitly give its holding period. The model assumes no borrowing, reserve-cash requirement or transaction costs; all available cash is assigned to projects. The budget constraints below prevent spending a payoff before it arrives.
$$A_1+D_1=100$$
$$A_2+C+D_2=1.06D_1$$
$$A_3+B+D_3=1.15A_1+1.06D_2$$
$$A_4+D_4=1.15A_2+1.06D_3$$
$$D_5=1.15A_3+1.40C+1.06D_4$$
$$0\le B\le40,\quad0\le C\le30,\quad A_t,D_t\ge0.$$
Maximize terminal wealth:
$$W=1.15A_4+1.25B+1.06D_5.$$
A 15% return means a 1.15 maturity multiplier, not 0.15. A flow diagram makes the timing clearer: an A investment skips one intermediate year boundary, while D links consecutive boundaries. With no cash reserve need and positive D returns, unused available funds can be put in D.

topics.warning: Page 26 is visibly blank. The displayed equations are a reader reconstruction: D is taken to mature after one year, quoted percentage returns are added to repaid principal, and maturity cash can be reinvested at year boundaries. The cash-flow diagram illustrates those same conventions; it is not copied from a completed lecture model.

topics.title: Data envelopment analysis: relative efficiency
topics.body: The visible pages 27-29 compare Alton, Beeks, Carey and Delancey elementary schools. Inputs are teacher/student ratio, supplementary funds per student and average parent education level; the slide explains education values 12 = high-school graduate and 16 = college graduate. Outputs are average reading, mathematics and history SOL test scores. The goal is to find schools that convert resources into outcomes less efficiently than the others. The full school data are in the table below.

sections.title: Reader-derived DEA formulation and its convention
sections.body:
A single output/input ratio is inadequate when both sides have several measures in different units. DEA searches for nonnegative weights that give each evaluated school its most favorable efficiency score, while preventing any school from scoring above one under the same weights.
For school o, let vᵢ weight inputs and uᵣ weight outputs. The reader chooses an input-oriented, constant-returns-to-scale (CCR) multiplier model to illustrate the method:
$$\max\sum_r u_r y_{ro}$$
$$\sum_i v_i x_{io}=1,\qquad\sum_r u_r y_{rj}-\sum_i v_i x_{ij}\le0\quad\text{for every school }j,$$
$$u_r,v_i\ge0.$$
The normalization turns the fractional efficiency ratio into a linear program. Solve separately for each school. A value below one indicates relative inefficiency under this chosen model; a value of one alone is not a claim that every input and output is individually efficient, especially when zero weights or slacks are allowed.
The slides do not specify a returns-to-scale convention on the blank formulation page. The displayed CCR convention is a reader choice, not a uniquely specified lecture model. Adding restrictions on weights or choosing variable returns produces a different DEA model.

sections.title: Derived comparison of the observed data
sections.body:
Alton uses no more of any input than Delancey (0.06 vs 0.06; 260 vs 460; 11.3 vs 13.1) and produces at least as much of every output (86 vs 81; 75 vs 73; 71 vs 69). Delancey is therefore dominated in the observed data. DEA is a comparison within the modeled set, not a causal explanation of school performance.
The closing slide cites an American Red Cross application integrating Excel, Access and Visual Basic to evaluate chapters with DEA. It illustrates turning many optimization models into a decision-support application.

topics.warning: Page 30 is visibly blank. It does not specify a returns-to-scale convention or display a completed DEA formulation. The reader’s CCR model and domination discussion are labeled deductions, not an official score table from the professor.

topics.title: Uncertain returns: what the last slide does and does not specify
topics.body: The final visible slide repeats the $100,000, five-year investment example with random returns. A can start in years 1-4 and pays after two years: 25% return with probability 20%, or 12.5% with probability 80%. B starts in year 3, pays at the end of year 5, and is capped at $40,000: the listed outcomes are a 30% return with probability 40% and 60% with probability 21.67%. C starts in year 2, pays at the end of year 4 and is capped at $30,000: its outcomes are 45% with probability 90% and -5% with probability 10%. D can be bought at the beginning of each year and gives 6%.

sections.title: Derived expected-return calculations
sections.body: A’s two probabilities sum to one, giving expected return 0.2(0.25) + 0.8(0.125) = 0.15. C’s expected return is 0.9(0.45) + 0.1(-0.05) = 0.40. For B, the listed probabilities total only 0.6167, leaving probability 0.3833 unexplained. The listed terms contribute 0.4(0.30) + 0.2167(0.60) = 0.25002, but this is not a complete expectation without the omitted outcome.

sections.title: What the slide does not determine
sections.body: A stochastic optimization model would need B’s complete distribution, a stated objective for risk, and a description of how returns are jointly realized and observed before later investments. These are not supplied on page 32. A risk-neutral expected-terminal-wealth model is one possible extension, not a uniquely stated lecture formulation. Later decisions must use only information already observed and cash actually available. Substituting expected multipliers into every cash-balance equation does not automatically produce a valid multistage stochastic plan.

topics.warning: Page 32 leaves 38.33% of B’s probability mass unspecified. Do not invent a missing outcome, silently renormalize the two printed probabilities, or claim a unique stochastic optimum from the available slide.

Compare official answer keys with independently checked worked solutions.

topics.title: Assignment 1: six airport-shuttle pricing policies
topics.body:
A shuttle has 40 seats. Regular tickets are bought less than seven days ahead; advance tickets are bought at least seven days ahead, including exactly seven days, and are nonrefundable and unchangeable. Demand is deterministic, quantities are continuous, operating costs are ignored, and customers do not switch between the regular and advance streams. Choose fares so that all demand is served and total demand is at most 40; there is no additional rationing or overbooking decision.
$$D_W(p)=\begin{cases}54-1.5p&0\le p\le30,\\24-0.5p&30<p\le48,\\0&p>48,\end{cases}\qquad D_A(p)=48-2p,\quad0\le p\le24.$$
The original fares are pW = $36 and pA = $18. Calculate demands, revenue and load factor for the benchmark; then compare filling capacity, optimizing only the advance fare, optimizing both fares, adding a student fare, and optimizing all three fares. These are derived worked solutions; no official Assignment 1 answer key is available in the synced materials. Related lecture: Airline demand, segmentation and advance fares.

sections.title: (a)-(c) Benchmark, fill the shuttle, optimize the advance fare
sections.body: At pW = 36, regular demand is 6. (a) At pA = 18, advance demand is 12, giving 18 passengers, 45% load factor and $432 revenue. (b) Filling capacity requires 34 advance passengers, so pA = (48 - 34)/2 = $7. Revenue becomes 6(36) + 34(7) = $454. (c) With pW fixed, maximize 216 + pA(48 - 2pA), subject to 6 + 48 - 2pA <= 40. Thus pA >= 7; the concave quadratic peaks at pA = $12. Advance demand is 24, total demand is 30, load factor is 75%, and revenue is $504. Selling ten fewer seats than in (b) earns $50 more because the retained advance passengers pay a higher fare. Load factor alone is not the revenue objective.

sections.title: (d) Jointly optimize the two fares
sections.body:
On the branch pW <= 30, use pW = 36 - (2/3)qW and pA = 24 - qA/2. Maximize 36qW - (2/3)qW^2 + 24qA - qA^2/2, with qW + qA <= 40, 9 <= qW <= 54 and 0 <= qA <= 48. Capacity binds. Equal marginal revenues give qW = 156/7 and qA = 124/7, so pW = 148/7 = $21.14 and pA = 106/7 = $15.14. Revenue is 5176/7 = $739.43 and load factor is 100%. The chosen regular fare is correctly below 30.
For pW >= 30, regular revenue decreases from the branch boundary; the best boundary policy is pW = 30 and pA = 12, with 9 + 24 = 33 passengers and $558 revenue. For the strictly open branch pW > 30, $558 is the limiting supremum. Either comparison is below $739.43.

sections.title: (e) Introduce a student fare
sections.body:
The students were already part of regular demand, not an additional population. Nonstudents have DR(pR) = 24 - pR/2 for 0 <= pR <= 48, and students have DS(pS) = 30 - pS for 0 <= pS <= 30; both become zero above their price limits. Student eligibility is checked by ID and nonstudents cannot use the student fare. Equal prices at or below 30 reproduce the first branch of DW; above 30, student demand vanishes.
At pR = 30 and pS = 18, qR = 9 and qS = 12, leaving 19 seats for advance demand. Its unconstrained revenue optimum would sell 24 seats, so the capacity limit binds: qA = 19 and pA = $14.50. Total revenue is 270 + 216 + 275.50 = $761.50, $22.07 above (d). The fixed fares reserve demand of 21 seats regardless of the descriptive ordering of fare choices.

sections.title: (f) Jointly optimize all three fares
sections.body:
Use inverse demands pR = 48 - 2qR, pS = 30 - qS, pA = 24 - qA/2 and quantity bounds 0 <= qR <= 24, 0 <= qS <= 30, 0 <= qA <= 48. Maximize 48qR - 2qR^2 + 30qS - qS^2 + 24qA - qA^2/2 subject to qR + qS + qA <= 40. Unconstrained quantities total 51, so capacity binds. Equal marginal revenues are 48 - 4qR = 30 - 2qS = 24 - qA = 44/7.
The optimum is (qR,qS,qA) = (73/7,83/7,124/7), or approximately (10.43,11.86,17.71). Prices are (190/7,127/7,106/7), approximately ($27.14,$18.14,$15.14). Revenue is 5365/7 = $766.43. This is $27 above joint unsegmented pricing in (d), and $4.93 above fixed segmented fares in (e). Concavity makes the marginal-revenue solution globally optimal. Capacity is allocated until the gain from one more seat is equal across the three eligible groups.

topics.title: Assignment 2: bounded, unbounded and reversed objectives
topics.body: Problems 1, 2 and 4 ask for graphical solutions, including maximization versus minimization. Draw each boundary line, keep the indicated half-plane, and evaluate the feasible vertices. An unbounded feasible region does not by itself imply an unbounded objective; demonstrate an improving feasible direction. All variables are nonnegative. The results below agree with the official key and have been independently recomputed. Related lecture: Graphical solution and irregular LP outcomes.

sections.title: Problem 1: a bounded maximum
sections.body:
$$\max Z=5x_1+8x_2;\quad3x_1+5x_2\le50,\quad2x_1+4x_2\le40,\quad x_1\le8,\quad x_2\le10,\quad x_1,x_2\ge0.$$
The feasible polygon has vertices (0,0), (8,0), (8,5.2), (0,10). Their objective values are 0, 40, 81.6, 80. Thus the unique maximum is (8,5.2), Z = 81.6. Draw the boundary from (0,10) to (8,5.2); the first resource and x1 bound meet at the optimum.

sections.title: Problem 2: unbounded maximum, finite minimum
sections.body:
$$Z=3x_1+2x_2;\quad2x_1+4x_2\ge22,\quad-x_1+4x_2\ge10,\quad4x_1-2x_2\le14,\quad x_1-3x_2\le1,\quad x_1,x_2\ge0.$$
The lower boundary vertices are (0,5.5), (4,3.5), and (38/7,27/7), with Z = 11, 19, and 24. The feasible region extends upward; increasing x2 with x1 fixed remains feasible and increases Z, proving the maximum is unbounded. Reversing to minimization gives (0,5.5), Z = 11.

sections.title: Problem 4: a triangular feasible region
sections.body:
$$Z=800x_1+900x_2;\quad2x_1+4x_2\le30,\quad4x_1+2x_2\le30,\quad x_1+x_2\ge9,\quad x_1,x_2\ge0.$$
The three vertices are (3,6), (5,5), and (6,3), with Z = $7,800, $8,500, and $7,500. The maximum is (5,5), $8,500; the minimum is (6,3), $7,500. Changing the objective sense changes the supporting corner, not the feasible triangle.

topics.title: Assignment 2: staffing permanent and temporary claim processors
topics.body: Problem 3 asks for an LP formulation and graphical solution. Permanent operators process 16 claims/day, produce 0.5 erroneous claims/day and cost $64/day. Temporary operators process 12 claims/day, produce 1.4 errors/day and cost $42/day. At least 450 claims must be processed, at most 40 workstations are available, and no more than 25 erroneous claims are allowed daily. Use continuous staffing quantities for the stated LP; integer hiring would be a different model. Related lecture: LP formulation and graphical solution.

sections.title: Model and feasible polygon
sections.body:
Let x1 and x2 be permanent and temporary operators.
$$\min Z=64x_1+42x_2;\quad16x_1+12x_2\ge450,\quad x_1+x_2\le40,\quad0.5x_1+1.4x_2\le25,\quad x_1,x_2\ge0.$$
Shade above the processing requirement and below the workstation and error limits. The feasible vertices are (28.125,0), (40,0), (34.444444,5.555556), and (20.121951,10.670732). Their daily costs are $1,800, $2,560, $2,437.777778, and $1,735.975610, respectively.

sections.title: Optimal staffing and source correction
sections.body: The processing and error constraints bind at the optimum: (x1,x2) = (20.1219512195,10.6707317073), with minimum cost $1,735.98/day after rounding to cents. Total staffing is about 30.792683, below 40. The official key identifies the same optimum. Its rounded cost label and one nonoptimal corner label need the corrections noted below.

topics.title: Assignment 3: aluminum mills and cost sensitivity
topics.body: For every Assignment 3 problem, parts (a)-(d) require a graphical solution, graphical coefficient sensitivity, algebraic sensitivity with slack/surplus variables, and Excel Solver verification. Mill 1 produces high/medium/low aluminum at 6/2/4 tons per day; Mill 2 produces 2/2/10. Requirements are at least 12/8/5 tons. Operating costs are $6,000 and $7,000 per day. Related lecture: Objective-coefficient ranges, slack and surplus variables, and Solver reports.

sections.title: (a) Formulation and vertices
sections.body:
Let x1,x2 be operating days.
$$\min Z=6000x_1+7000x_2;\quad6x_1+2x_2\ge12,\quad2x_1+2x_2\ge8,\quad4x_1+10x_2\ge5,\quad x_1,x_2\ge0.$$
The low-grade row is redundant. The unbounded feasible region lies above the high- and medium-grade boundaries. Vertices (0,6), (1,3), and (4,0) cost $42,000, $27,000, and $24,000. The minimum is four days at Mill 1 and zero at Mill 2.

sections.title: (b)-(c) Graphical and algebraic sensitivity
sections.body:
The objective slope is -c1/c2. At (4,0), adjacent boundary slopes are -1 and 0, so 0 <= c1 <= c2 keeps this corner optimal. With c2 = 7,000, c1 ranges from 0 to 7,000 (allowable decrease 6,000; increase 1,000). With c1 = 6,000, c2 ranges from 6,000 to infinity (decrease 1,000; unlimited increase).
Introduce surplus variables e1,e2,e3 by subtracting them from the three >= rows. The nonbasic variables are x2 and e2.
$$x_1=4-x_2+\tfrac12e_2,\quad e_1=12-4x_2+3e_2,\quad e_3=11+6x_2+2e_2.$$
$$Z=24000+1000x_2+3000e_2=4c_1+(c_2-c_1)x_2+\tfrac12c_1e_2.$$
For minimization, both nonbasic coefficients must remain nonnegative, giving exactly 0 <= c1 <= c2. At the original costs they are strictly positive, proving the unique optimum. Range endpoints can have multiple optima.

sections.title: (d) Solver verification
sections.body: For part (d), enter decision cells, a SUMPRODUCT objective and constraint left-hand sides, choose Simplex LP and nonnegative variables, then request the Sensitivity Report. Compare its solution and coefficient ranges with the values here. The official key provides the analytical solution but no actual Excel report; the report checks below are independently derived expectations, not a claim that Excel was run. Expected original-row shadow prices (high, medium, low) are ($0,$3,000,$0) per ton. The variable reduced costs are (0,$1,000). Medium demand can decrease from 8 to 4 with the same basis and has no finite upper bound; the high and low rows have current surpluses 12 and 11.
